archetype.name: Playoff Team (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose record is backed by a top-three net efficiency, built almost entirely on Joe Burrow's passing game and a pass rush that wins on obvious downs, with a run game and run defense that are along for the ride.

report.headline: Burrow's passing game is the real thing; the defense's red-zone stands are shakier.
report.take:
This is Burrow's team in the purest sense. Cincinnati passes more than any offense in the league relative to the situation, and it earns that lean: the pass offense ranks 4th in EPA per play and the offense as a whole is 2nd in success rate. Every week the run game posts negative EPA in the box score except at Pittsburgh, and it ranks 22nd in rush EPA on a 3.6 yards-per-carry clip. The line's run blocking is quietly functional (4th-lowest stuff rate, 3rd in short-yardage conversion), so the ground game moves the chains when asked but rarely breaks anything. The offense is a high-volume, high-efficiency dropback machine with Chase and Higgins splitting targets evenly and Chase Brown as a real receiving outlet.

The record is earned, not lucky. At 5-2 with a 48-point differential, the point differential implies 4.6 wins, a 50% one-score record is neutral, and the net EPA ranks 3rd. That is a contender's profile on paper, and the bigger story is how far the defense has come. A unit that ranked 29th in EPA allowed last season and 27th the year before is now 12th, almost entirely because of the pass rush: 21 sacks (2nd), a 27.2% pressure rate (5th) and the 2nd-best sack rate. Against the deep ball it ranks 6th.

What the numbers hide is how much bend there is. Opponents convert 48.1% of third downs (30th), the defense misses tackles at a 25th-ranked rate, gives up explosive runs often (26th) and gets carved underneath (27th in short-pass EPA, 30th against tight ends). It survives because it allows touchdowns on only 35% of red-zone trips, 3rd in the league, a rate that rarely holds for a defense that lets drives live this long. The Tennessee game, 36 points allowed to the league's 26th-ranked offense, is what it looks like when the red zone stops don't arrive. The turnover cushion is thinner than it looked, too: the takeaway bursts against Tampa Bay and Miami were offset by four giveaways against the Titans, leaving the season turnover margin at just +1.

So the shape going forward is a team that should keep winning a lot of games through its quarterback while giving up more points than its early red-zone numbers suggest. The schedule helps, with Washington, New Orleans, Carolina and Indianapolis still ahead, but Pittsburgh next week and a trip to Cleveland decide the division. Expect shootouts more than blowouts.

strengths.title: An elite, pass-first offense
strengths.body: Cincinnati leans on the pass harder than anyone in the league and remains efficient at volume, ranking 4th in pass EPA and 2nd in success rate. Burrow has thrown for 2,115 yards with two receivers at 61 targets each, so defenses can't roll coverage to one side. With a stable starting quarterback and the 7th-best sack rate allowed, this is the most sustainable part of the team.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: The rush ranks 5th in pressure rate and turns that pressure into sacks at the league's 2nd-best rate, which is what flipped this defense from bottom-five last season to above average now. Pressure tends to be stickier than coverage or turnover luck, so this should travel. It also explains why the pass defense is strong deep while it gets nickel-and-dimed short.

strengths.title: A record backed by efficiency
strengths.body: Net EPA ranks 3rd, the point differential implies 4.6 wins against five actual, and the one-score record is a neutral .500. Nothing about the 5-2 start depends on close-game magic.

concerns.title: Third downs and red-zone luck
concerns.body: The defense lets opponents convert 48.1% of third downs (30th) and misses tackles too often, yet it allows touchdowns on only 35% of red-zone trips (3rd). That combination usually breaks toward more points allowed, because long drives eventually end in touchdowns. Tennessee's 36 points were a preview.

concerns.title: Soft underneath and against runs
concerns.body: Teams beat this defense with quick throws, tight ends and runs that break the second level. It ranks 27th in short-pass EPA, 30th against the opposing TE1 and 26th in explosive run rate allowed. A starting corner on the injury report makes the underneath problem worse.

concerns.title: A run game that can't close
concerns.body: At 3.6 yards a carry and 22nd in rush EPA, the ground game can't reliably bleed a lead, which is part of why games like Tennessee turned into shootouts. This is a structural trait, not a slump, and it puts extra weight on Burrow protecting the ball.

trend.note: The passing game has been dominant for most of the season, posting double-digit pass EPA in four of the last five games, including a 35-13 rout in Baltimore. The worry is the latest result: the defense gave up 36 to a weak Tennessee offense in a game Cincinnati only survived.

nextGame.headline: Burrow against a thinned Falcons secondary; ATL's run game is the threat.
nextGame.body:
Atlanta is a 3-5 team with an above-average defense (8th in play-by-play EPA) and a bottom-five passing offense, so it lives on the run: it passes well below expectation, averages 4.82 yards a carry (3rd) and protects Michael Penix Jr. well, with the league's lowest pressure rate allowed. That sets up a clash of styles. Cincinnati wants a dropback game and a lead, while Atlanta wants long, run-heavy drives that keep Burrow on the sideline and expose the Bengals' third-down problem. The Book has Cincinnati -3 on the road with a 52.5 total, which expects points.

Availability tilts toward Cincinnati. Atlanta is without linebacker Divine Deablo (83% of snaps), corner Billy Bowman Jr., edge Samson Ebukam, back Brian Robinson Jr. and receiver Zachariah Branch, which thins both the coverage and the pass rush Burrow faces. On the Bengals' side, the one that matters is corner DJ Turner II, a 95%-snap starter listed questionable and day-to-day with an ankle. Edge rushers Cashius Howell and Cedric Johnson are also questionable, safety Kyle Dugger is out, and tight end Erick All Jr. is done for the season.

waysToWin.title: Feed the second receiver and Brown
waysToWin.body: Atlanta's defense has been worst-in-class against secondary options, ranking 29th in EPA allowed to the opposing WR2 and 30th against the lead back. With Chase and Higgins splitting targets evenly and Chase Brown a frequent target, Burrow can live in those matchups, especially with Deablo and Bowman out.

waysToWin.title: Get ahead and make Penix throw
waysToWin.body: Atlanta's pass offense ranks 29th in EPA, and the team avoids throwing for a reason. An early lead forces Penix into dropbacks where Cincinnati's sack rate, 2nd in the league, can end drives, even against a line that keeps pressure down.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden margins
waysToWin.body: Atlanta's special teams rank 29th in EPA, and the Falcons haven't won a one-score game. If this one is close late, field position and Atlanta's track record in tight finishes lean Cincinnati's way.

waysToLose.title: Atlanta grinds out long drives
waysToLose.body: A top-three rushing offense against a defense that misses tackles, allows explosive runs and can't get off the field on third down is the clearest upset script. If Atlanta controls the clock and turns those drives into touchdowns, the Bengals' red-zone luck runs out and Burrow gets fewer possessions.

waysToLose.title: Another giveaway day
waysToLose.body: Four turnovers nearly cost Cincinnati the Tennessee game, and the season margin is down to +1. Atlanta's defense has 10 takeaways, and short fields would let a limited offense score without beating the Bengals' pass rush.

waysToLose.title: Turner sits, underneath opens
waysToLose.body: Cincinnati already ranks 27th against short passes. Without a 95%-snap corner, even a struggling passer can move the ball on quick, safe throws that pair with the run game.

nextGame.watch: Atlanta's third-down conversions on its run-heavy drives: if the Bengals get off the field, Burrow's volume against a depleted defense should decide it.

restOfSeason.body:
The passing offense is the bankable piece: stable quarterback play, two target-equal receivers and efficiency that ranks near the top of the league in both EPA and success rate. Expect it to keep producing close to its current level, with Iosivas' possible return adding depth and All's season-ending injury taking some away at tight end. The defense is where regression lives. A 30th-ranked third-down defense and middling tackling won't keep holding opponents to touchdowns on a third of red-zone trips, so points allowed should drift up from the early pace. The pass rush gives it a floor well above last season's unit.

The schedule is forgiving overall, with Washington, New Orleans, Carolina and Indianapolis all sitting at or below .500, but the division runs through Pittsburgh at home next week and two games with Cleveland, plus Kansas City at home. A team this efficient should finish around double-digit wins and contend for the division. How it fares in the four games against Pittsburgh, Cleveland and Kansas City decides whether it hosts a playoff game.
swingFactors: Whether the red-zone defense holds up as third downs keep leaking
DJ Turner II's ankle and the depth at edge rusher

confidence.note: Seven games with a stable QB and a clear identity, but the defense rests on red-zone and takeaway rates that rarely hold.
